title: Planning ahead
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart's contention is that the cheapest available improvement in most schools is not curriculum or pedagogy but organisation, and specifically the discipline of planning ahead. He sets the problem up as a clash of timescales: complex problems such as budget deficits or falling enrolment take years, future problems such as demographics, competitors, technology and regulation take longer still, and both compete with the daily firefighting of school leadership. His answer is an annual rhythm that gives future thinking a home while providing present clarity, nested inside a monthly rhythm that locks in the fixed points first - governance meetings, audits, surveys, data collection, lesson observations and book looks, SEF writing, then the improvement cycle and the CPL programme that follows from the priorities. Once out-of-hours demands such as parents' evenings and reports are mapped too, the pattern of overloaded and empty months becomes visible and can be interrogated: what must stay, what can move, what survives only because we always do it then. He then makes the artefact operational by proposing planning ahead as a standing SLT agenda item, with worked preparation lists for an assessment point, a book look and parents' evenings. The claimed return is fewer surprises for teachers, more meaningful CPL, and leadership attention shifting from firefighting to sense-making.
points: Hart argues for planning backwards from accountability dates, since governance and regulatory deadlines are the genuinely immovable anchors that everything else should be scheduled around.
The diagnostic question is not what the calendar contains but which rhythms actually support improvement and which survive only from habit.
Making the year plan a standing SLT item converts a document into a practice, which is what separates this from the usual mapping exercise.
His worked example for book looks - purpose, sampling, cover, feedback routes, communication, a sense-check with trusted colleagues - is presented as trust protection, not just logistics.
The underlying claim is that organisation buys leadership bandwidth: last-minute scrambles consume exactly the attention that complex and future problems require.
quotes: I am convinced that most schools can improve by being more organised. Yes, we can and should seek to refine our curriculum, our pedagogical approach and the way that we lead behaviour, but the relatively low hanging fruit is organisation and planning ahead.

Complex problems such as reducing a budget deficit, sustainably increasing enrollment or introducing new curricula can take years. And we also need to consider future problems such as those related to population data, the performance of competitors, the development of new technologies, the maturity of regulation frameworks, the employment landscape and the needs of our community.

The school year has distinct phases. Planning ahead involves what the school pays attention to and the work it does at different times of year to tackle its complex problems and consider its future problems.

Schools can easily become overwhelmingly busy at different points of the year if we do not deliberately schedule key events. So where do we start? We might start with planning ahead for accountability requirements.
Once all of these demands for our attention are mapped, patterns appear. Some months are too heavy while others are curiously empty.

Imagine that every significant cultural and operational artefact is mapped by month, aligned to the phases of the year and spaced in a way that avoids crunch points. How do we use it? The simplest and most powerful move is to make the plan a standing item at SLT meetings: planning ahead.
